full_judgment:
2. Facts of these two cases are simple and they are briefly given below: Ashutosh, one of the two original defendants and husband of respondent Hiran Bala Devi, entered into an oral contract with appellant Rash Behari, to sell his part of the suit property namely, a house, for a consideration of Tk. 6,000/- on 15 April 1969 and received the entire consideration in three instalments, but did not execute the necessary conveyance. Thereupon Rash Behari filed Title Suit No.192 of 1970 seeking specific performance of the contract. Similarly, respondent Anima Devi, widow of Ashutosh Chakraborty's brother, entered into art oral Agreement on the same day with Chintarni, wife of Rash Behari, to sell her share of the suit property for a consideration of Tk. 6,000/- and received the entire amount in three installments but did not execute the necessary conveyance whereupon Chintarani filed Title Suit No.193 of 1970 for specific performance of the contract. Both the suits were heard analogously by the learned Munsif. The contracts were not challenged by the defendants, but payment of consideration was totally denied. The trial Court found on evidence that though the contracts were proved to be lawful no consideration was at all paid. But, nevertheless, the trial Court decreed the suits by a common judgment on 28 February 1974 subject to payment of the consideration. The defendants challenged the decrees by filing two separate appeals-Title Appeals Nos.88 and 89 of 1974. Both the appeals were dismissed by the learned Subordinate Judge by a common judgment dated 30 August 1975 whereupon second appeals, being Nos.54 and 55 of 1976, were filed challenging the decrees. These appeals were allowed, the decrees were set aside and the suits were dismissed by a learned Single Judge by the impugned judgment dated 28 February 1982. on the findings that the plaintiffs not only did not pay a single farthing by way of consideration but put up a false claim of payment and that they were not willing and ready to per-form their part of the contract. 

 3. Mr. S.R. Pal. learned Advocate for the plaintiffs-appellants has seriously assailed the High Court Division's order refusing specific performance of the contracts which were proved to be lawful contracts between the parties. The learned Advocate has referred to section 22 of the Specific Relief Act which provides that the Court's jurisdiction to decree specific performance is discretionary, and has pointed out that though it is discretionary, the discretion of the Court is not arbitrary but sound and reasonable, guided by judicial principles. The learned Advocate is of the opinion that the learned Single Judge arbitrarily exercised his jurisdiction in reversing the concurrent decision of the trial Court and the lower Appellate Court which decreed the specific performance of the contract.
